title: Autonomous Region of Bougainville
description: Autonomous region of Papua New Guinea
wiki_lead:
Bougainville (, BOH-gən-vil; Tok Pisin: Bogenvil), officially the Autonomous Region of Bougainville (Tok Pisin: Otonomos Rijen bilong Bogenvil), is an autonomous region in Papua New Guinea. The largest island is Bougainville Island, while the region also includes Buka Island and a number of outlying islands and atolls. The provisional capital is Buka, on Buka Island.
In 2024, the region had a population of 367,093 people. The lingua franca of Bougainville is Tok Pisin, while a variety of Austronesian and non-Austronesian languages are also spoken. The region includes several Polynesian outliers where Polynesian languages are spoken. Geographically, the islands of Bougainville and Buka form part of the Solomon Islands archipelago, but they are politically separate from the independent country of Solomon Islands. Historically, Bougainville and Buka, together with the islands of Choiseul, Santa Isabel, the Shortlands, and Ontong Java, which are all now part of the country of Solomon Islands, formed the German Solomon Islands Protectorate, the geographical area later being referred to as the North Solomon Islands.
Bougainville has been inhabited by humans for at least 29,000 years. During the colonial period, the region was occupied and administered by the Germans, Australians and Japanese for various periods. The name of the region originates from French admiral Louis Antoine de Bougainville, who reached it in 1768.
Bougainvillean separatism dates to the 1960s, and the Republic of the North Solomons was declared shortly before the independence of Papua New Guinea in 1975; it was subsumed into Papua New Guinea the following year. Conflict over the Panguna mine became the primary trigger for the Bougainville Civil War (1988–1998), which resulted in the deaths of up to 20,000 people. A peace agreement resulted in the creation of the Autonomous Bougainville Government.
In late 2019, a non-binding independence referendum was held with 98% voting for independence rather than continued autonomy within Papua New Guinea. As a result, the regional authorities intend to become independent by 2027, pending ratification by the Papua New Guinean government. If ratified, the capital may relocate from Buka back to the previous location of Arawa. In March 2025, the Bougainville Independence Leaders Consultation Forum recommended 1 September 2027 as the date of independence, a date later revised in July 2026 to 1 September 2030.

History


Prehistory
Bougainville has been inhabited by humans for at least 29,000 years, according to evidence obtained from Kilu Cave on Buka Island. grok_lead: The Autonomous Region of Bougainville is an autonomous entity within Papua New Guinea, consisting of Bougainville Island, Buka Island, and numerous smaller islets in the northern Solomon Islands archipelago, covering approximately 9,384 square kilometers with a population estimated at around 300,000 primarily of Melanesian descent. Its capital is Buka Town, and the region features diverse terrain including rainforests, volcanic mountains like Mount Balbi at 2,715 meters, and coastal ecosystems supporting traditional livelihoods. Granted autonomy under the 2001 Bougainville Peace Agreement following a civil war that claimed 15,000 to 20,000 lives, the Autonomous Bougainville Government exercises control over local administration, fiscal policy, and development, while national defense and foreign affairs remain under Papua New Guinea's jurisdiction. The Bougainville conflict originated in the late 1980s from local grievances against the environmental and social impacts of the Panguna copper-gold mine, operated by a foreign consortium, which prompted the formation of the Bougainville Revolutionary Army and the mine's closure in 1989, escalating into a secessionist insurgency against Papua New Guinea forces. The decade-long war involved factional fighting, a national blockade, and widespread disruption, culminating in the peace accord that established a framework for autonomy and a future referendum on political status. Post-conflict reconstruction has focused on restoring governance and economy, though the region remains heavily reliant on subsistence agriculture, cocoa and copra exports, with the dormant Panguna mine representing both potential economic revival and renewed controversy over resource extraction rights. In line with the peace agreement, a referendum held from November 23 to December 7, 2019, offered voters the choice between greater autonomy or independence, resulting in 176,928 votes (97.7%) for independence out of 180,971 valid ballots. The non-binding outcome requires ratification by Papua New Guinea's National Parliament, a process stalled as of 2025 due to debates over Bougainville's fiscal sustainability and shared resource interests, including deep-sea mining prospects in its exclusive economic zone. This unresolved status underscores ongoing negotiations aimed at balancing self-determination aspirations with practical integration challenges.
